Oṃ, salutations to Śaṅkara, whose self is the Bhairava of Consciousness. Now.
The *Vijñānabhairava*, accompanied by the commentary *Vijñānakaumudī* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭānanda.
[Salutation to] Śrīvidyā, Maheśa in the form of Śrīkaṇṭha.
Somānanda, Bhūtirāja, and Utpaleśa—
those who descended into the world of mortals for the sake of reviving the Śiva scriptures that had set with the passage of time. (1)
Those like me, who have perceived reality in the mirror of the mind whose mire has been washed away by speech, body, and mental activity through the pollen of the lotus feet of that Name upon Name—
These [works] shine eternally in the assemblies of the virtuous. (A pair of verses.
[I bow to] the venerable Lakṣmaṇa, Abhinavagupta, and others, who are moons for the great ocean of the instruction on the reality of the meaning of Trika.

Having meditated upon the gurus, who possess the radiance of the rising sun that causes the lotus of the dull-witted heart to bloom, and who have rendered the path of the world free from darkness; || 3 ||
By observing the other side of the hidden path through the meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) emerging from the lotus-face of Śarva, one is protected at every step,
even while stumbling.
This is the *Padadīpikā* on the system of the *Vijñānabhairava*. (A pair of verses.
Herein, Bhairava himself, the author of this scripture, [describes] through various internal and external forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth...

Having concealed its own nature through various purposeful activities (*arthakriyā*), and then having emerged outward like a mass of sunbeams, the devotees should, by means of this path of knowledge, again enter [the source] through the realization of their own true nature and attain identity with it— this is the intended purpose.
Through the door of the powers of the expansion of her own consciousness, such as knowledge and action, she speaks in the form of the questioner; thus [it is said]:
"The venerable Bhairavī said," and so forth.
"O Lord, I have heard everything that was spoken in the *Yāmala* and other scriptures—the entirety of the three divisions, categorized according to their essence and sub-essence. (1)
Even now, O Supreme Lord, my doubt has not ceased:
what, in reality, O God, is that form which consists of the essence of the multitude of sounds? (2)
Or what is the use of the ninefold division of the self within Bhairava, who is of the form of Bhairava?
Or what is the use of that which is divided by the Triśirobheda, or that which consists of the three powers?
Is it composed of *nāda* and *bindu*, or is it that which obstructs the half-moon?
Is it mounted upon the *cakras*, devoid of phonemes (*anacka*), or is it the very nature of *Śakti*? (4)
Whether it belongs to the Parāparā or the Aparā, if it were likewise [identical] to the Parā, then its status as "higher" (paratva) would be contradicted. || 5 ||
Supremacy does not arise from a distinction of caste nor from a distinction of body;
it does not arise through being partless (niṣkala) nor through being with parts (sakala).

3) O Lord, grant me grace; completely sever my doubt regarding whatever is found in the scriptures, such as the *Yāmala* and others, which have as their essential cause the union of Śiva and Śakti.

Whatever has been heard from your mouth regarding the *Yāmalas* known as the *Brahma*, *Viṣṇu*, *Rudra*, and *Bhairava*, as well as the *Āgamas* bearing those names— all that exists as already previously heard through the logical proof of their unity;
by the maxim of a reflection in a mirror, it is either not distinct from that [source] or indeed distinct, yet internally it is one in its unity.

And externally, by way of being composed of the triad of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva, this has been heard and previously understood both as the uncommon and the common; yet even now, my doubt does not cease,
because [the universe] is congealed within the nature of Bhairavī, which is the nature of the powers beginning with Māyā.

[The disciple says: "There is no cessation of doubt regarding her—my identity with you has not yet been established even now"—this is the sense. Because she unfolds from being firmly attached to the wall of one's own self, she is the "bearer of the universe" (*viśvabhṛtrī*) by virtue of being identical with the universe everywhere.

The determination of the truth regarding the questions and answers, as well as the exposition of the essential nature of the union (*yāmala*) consisting of the identity (*sāmarasya*) of Bhairavī and Bhairava,
has been explained at length in works such as the *Tantrāloka* and the *Parātriṃśikā*; it is not elaborated upon by us here.

Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of being a secret thief [of the teaching], let us return to the subject at hand—the sense is: "Tell me what, in reality and in truth, is the nature of that which is of the form of the Absolute (anuttara). In this regard, is it of the nature of the totality of phonemes (śabdarāśi-kalā), or is it of the nature of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman)?

"One who is proficient in the Śabdabrahman attains the Supreme Brahman. Alternatively, [the term] may signify "A" through the phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, or "I" (*ahaṃ*) as one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), or "Akṣa" as the Self (*ātman*), or else as the essence of the nine principles (*navatattva*), or as the nature of the nine powers (*śakti*) such as Vāmā and the rest.

In Bhairava— that is, in the consciousness-principle (cittattva) which consists of the fivefold cosmic functions, whose form is that of Bhairava, whose nature is the full state of "I-am-ness" (pūrṇāhaṃbhāva) characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda).

That reality is either divided according to the threefold division of the Triśirobhedha as the self of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva; or else it consists of the threefold operation of the subject, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; or again, it consists of the operation of the three powers beginning with Will (icchā), and is composed of Nāda and Bindu.
Or rather, by means of the nature of the powers of knowledge and action— which consist of the word and cognition whose essence is Śiva and Śakti—
or through the activity consisting of the *praṇava*, the *aṅgamantra*, the *māyā*, the *ardhacandra*, and the *nirodhinī*,
one perceives that certain reality (*tattva*) situated within the six-petaled and other cakras, which manifests as the three-and-a-half coils in the form of Kuṇḍalinī.

I am the radiance of the nature mounted upon the wheel [of letters] beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣ*; or, being "without vowels" (*anacka*), I am the form consisting of the consonants from *ka* to *kṣa*, devoid of the sixteen vowels starting with *a*—that is, my own nature is *ka kha ga gha ṅa*, and so forth;
and furthermore, [my mantra is] "Oṃ namaḥ śrīvidyāpādukābhyaḥ."
Is that form which is joined with vowels and consonants yet devoid of articulated sound— that partless form "a u m na maḥ rī vidyā pādakābhyaḥ"—

is that indeed the nature of the supreme speech (*parā-vāk*), or the nature of the intermediate speech (*aparā-vāk*), or the nature of the speech that is both supreme and intermediate (*parāparā-vāk*)? Tell me all this.

For the supreme power is indeed the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*); that same power, desiring to create succession, becomes the lower (*aparā*), and being in the form of succession, it is called the "both supreme and lower" (*parāparā*). Thus, in the *Tantrāloka*, it is said:
"The power of absolute freedom is the desire to emit succession."
And the nature of succession— this is the sovereign power of the All-pervasive One.
That very triad of Goddesses, abiding within,
manifests my own unsurpassed essential nature.

By such statements as these: because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between the nature of the *aparā* and the *parāparā*, if the *parā* were also exactly like them, its status as *parā* (the supreme) would be contradicted. Since the distinction between the *parāparā* and the *aparā* is established through their difference, that *paratva* (supremacy) would be contradicted in the *parā-svarūpa* (the essential nature of the supreme) due to the inherent nature of non-difference (*abhedasvabhāva*) therein; thus it is so.

The sense is that, within the Supreme (Parā), everything belonging to the nature of both the higher-lower (parāparā) and the lower (aparā)—namely, the entire aggregate of objects of knowledge—would be contradicted; for [in Parā] there is non-differentiation from That (the Absolute). On this point, in the Supreme...

"This is contradictory because of [the doctrine of] rebirth; for that Supreme Reality could not possess such diversity—whether through the distinctions of Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra, and so forth, nor through the distinction of bodies, nor through the various bodily compositions of gods, humans, animals, and so on—neither by being partless (niṣkala) nor by being with parts (sakala). Thus [he asks].
Through the unification of speech, body, and mind, grant me your grace; bestow upon me the vision of grace.

By means of such contemplations as "What is this? What is this? and so forth—having abandoned everything through the touch of the single peak (ekakoṭi), through the relinquishing of outward orientation, or through the avoidance of the object of knowledge (prameya)—one should cultivate the sense of "I" as the reality of the knower (pramātṛ-tattva).
The sense is: "Establish that very reality which is the subject (pramātṛtattva). Furthermore, regarding the doubt in my heart—"Is this it? Is that it? What is this? Or what is that?
Is it otherwise?"—and so forth, while I am in a state of duality, speak a definitive conclusion: that there is only one reality of the subject, which is self-luminous.

Show that very [reality] to me, by which—through the logic of the reflection in a mirror and because everything is shown not to exceed one's own self—the non-difference [of all things] is established; and through this realization of non-difference, there may arise the certain conviction: "I am," resting in one's own essential nature, and "all this is my own nature. *Prasāda* is the act of bringing [something] into a state of excellence (*prakarsa*).
The intended meaning is: "Compose the reasoning that establishes the identity with one's own self by means of the removal of difference and the proof of non-difference. || 1-6 ||

Thus, having been questioned in the form of Bhairavī, who is non-different from His own self-consciousness, the Supreme Lord Himself— the teacher of the Siddhānta and the one established in the definitive position regarding the scriptures on the principles (tattvas)—
Bhairava spoke.

By these and other such statements, the meaning of the word *bhairava* therein has been previously established in the word *bhairavī*, which is indicated as having an essence non-different from it. Furthermore, he is called *bhairava* because he protects (*avati*) [beings] from what is terrifying (*bhīma*) and so forth; the sense is that through the manifestation of "I" (*aham*), the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*) is destroyed, like frozen snow or ghee. Thus he "spoke" (*uvāca*).
Having brought face-to-face the power of consciousness whose nature is non-different from Himself, He promises:
"Excellent, excellent! O beloved, you have asked about this essence of the Tantra."
(6) O auspicious lady, although it is most secret, I shall nevertheless tell you:
whatever form of Bhairava has been proclaimed in its entirety.
Therefore, O Goddess, it should be understood as being without essence, like a magical illusion, comparable to a dream and a mirage, and like the wandering of a city of the Gandharvas. 9.
For those of deluded intellect who engage in a mere display of ritual actions,
meditation has been described solely for the sake of men whose very selves are destroyed by conceptual construction.
In reality, he is not the ninefold self, nor is he the mass of sounds, nor Bhairava;
nor is he the three-headed god, nor is he composed of the triple energy.
It consists neither of sound nor of the drop (nāda-bindu), nor does it obstruct the half-moon;
it is not differentiated by the sequence of the wheels (cakras), nor is it of the nature of power (śakti). || 12 ||
For those of unawakened minds, these are indeed terrors for the childish;
everything has been taught for the sake of engagement, like a mother’s sweetmeat. 13.
Transcending the measurement of space and time, undifferentiated by location or direction, she cannot be designated; in the ultimate sense, she is ineffable.
That state of the Bhairava-self, which consists of the bliss of internal self-experience, whose sphere is liberated from conceptual construction, and which is full in form—that is Bhairavī. (15)
That body should be known in its true essence as stainless and filling the universe.
In such a supreme reality, who is there to be worshipped, and who is there to be satisfied? (16)
In this way, whatever state of Bhairava is celebrated, that is proclaimed as the Supreme Goddess (Parā Devī) in her form as both the supreme and the non-supreme (parāpara). (17)
Since the non-difference between power and the possessor of power is eternally established, the Supreme Power belongs to the Supreme Self by virtue of being His attribute and its substratum. (18)

The burning power of fire is not perceived as distinct from the fire itself; this [notion of] "commencement" is merely a designation for the entry [of the power] into the existence of consciousness. (19)
For one who has entered the state of Śakti, there is meditation without differentiation;
at that time, he becomes identical with Śiva, and this is here called the "Śaiva mouth. (20)
Just as the divisions of the directions and so forth are known by the light of a lamp or by the rays of the sun, even so [the powers] of Śiva are known through His power.

"O Goddess, that which has been asked by you is excellent, excellent; because it is the supreme goal, the instruction is excellent, excellent. As for the fact that you have asked for the essence of the determinations of the tantras, the sense is that this must be concealed within yourself and meditated upon as non-different from one's own self, but not expressed through speech such as *vaikharī* and so forth."

Even more than that, I too say it is not otherwise. And as for this well-known twofold form of Bhairava—both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*)—this entire form of the world, with its manifold variety of blue and non-blue objects such as jars and so forth, all of that is like a city of Gandharvas, equal to a magical illusion; this is the remainder [of the meaning]. Having enjoyed and having drunk...
In the statement "I slept happily," [the experience] is like a dream-vision and like a city of Gandharvas;
likewise, for those of unawakened minds, of deluded intellects,
who abide in the intentionality toward the fruits dominated by karma, [the teaching] "I am Viṣṇu" is for the purpose of the practice of gross meditation.

"I worship Gaṇapati; I worship him so that he will grant me a son"—this has been described for those men whose minds are struck down by such conceptualization. In reality, however, he is not the "Ninefold Self" (Navātman).

It is not the nature of the nine principles (*navatattva*), nor is it the nature of the nine powers such as *vāmā* and the rest; nor is it composed of the triad of *nara*, *śakti*, and *śiva*, nor is it the triad of the powers of will, knowledge, and action; nor is it the nature of *śiva* and *śakti*; nor is it the form of the concepts expressed by the words "nāda" [sound], "śakti" [power], and "bindu" [point], nor is it essentially knowledge and action.

It is not of the nature of the half-moon (ardhacandra) or the cessation (nirodha) called *amā*, nor does it reside within the divisions of the six chakras and so forth in the form of Kuṇḍalinī and the like; it is not the wheel of phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, nor is its essential nature the "I" (*ahaṃ*),
nor does it possess the nature of the power (śakti) of Kuṇḍalinī and the rest— except, that is, for those of deluded intellects.

These are terrors for children, intended for the pacification of dogmatic attachment and the like; for a child is indeed coaxed by means of terrors by his own mother. Furthermore, he is coaxed with the thought, "I shall give you a sweetmeat or sugar" so that he will consume medicine and such things. In this way, that supreme state—which existed beyond all reckoning regarding directions, times, and the elements—is [described].

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "I teach you that which—though undifferentiated by distinctions such as 'it exists' or 'it will exist,' or by being distant or near, and though impossible to teach—is indeed taught. This is the state of Bhairava, whose nature is full, consisting solely of self-luminosity and the non-conceptual ultimate reality;
it is the state of being filled with form (*bharitākāra*) belonging to Bhairava of the perfect nature, which consists of resting in the "I" (*aham*). That alone [is what is taught].

The sense is that the body should be understood as Bhairava. Thus, in this reality of Bhairava, who is the one to be worshipped, or who is satisfied, or who attains satisfaction? In this manner, the supreme state (*parāvasthā*) of Bhairava is proclaimed by means of this form.
And because there is non-duality between these two—the power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*)—this is called the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*). And here:

The illustration is as follows: just as the burning power of fire is not distinct from it, so too this Power (Śakti) is Supreme (Parā); the sense is that through this very means, there may be a face-to-face encounter with Bhairava. Furthermore, there is another illustration here:
for just as it is by means of the mouth alone that one is recognized as "this person," so too is the designation "this is Śiva" made possible solely by means of Power.

There is yet another illustration: just as the divisions of the directions and so forth are known through the light of a lamp or the radiance of the sun, even so is the manifestation of Śiva by means of power (śakti); thus it is established. || 7.21 ||
The illustrious Bhairavī said:
O God of gods, marked with the trident and adorned with a skull as an ornament!
It is devoid of direction, place, and time, and is free from all designations.
That power of Bhairava which is perceived as having a full form—
by what means is its mouth reached, and how does it become the Supreme Goddess?
O Lord, speak to me according to how I correctly understand it.

The Lord’s state of possessing a skull in his hand (*kapālapāṇitva*) is established by his essential existence, which is filled with the triad of powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action; and by his sustaining the universe through its withdrawal into himself, holding it as nothing but bones within his own being. Furthermore, [he is characterized by] emptiness in the ten directions, in space, in time, and in the primary elements (*bhūta*).

The remainder of the meaning is as follows: by what means may that face and the vision of it—which is characterized by the name "the beyond" (parā) due to its non-differentiation from That—come to be? And just as I exist as your own essential nature because of the logical possibility of non-difference from you, so speak for me:
lead me into that very state; such is the sense.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Prāṇa is indeed above and jīva is below; one should utter the supreme [syllable] which is the nature of emission.
Because it sustains [all things] at the two places of origin, its state is full.

Above, at the *dvādaśānta*, the *prāṇa*—which is of the nature of breathing and known as life-force (*jīvana*), being a particular modification of the mind’s activity (*cittavṛtti*)—is to be established; and below, in the heart—that is, in the region of the heart—the *jīva* is the *apāna*. It is called *jīva* because one lives by means of it; since it flows through the lower path for the purpose of eating, drinking, and so forth, it is termed *jīva*, and it is precisely because of this that it possesses those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

The term *jīva* refers to that whose self is the emission (*visarga*), whose nature consists of the internal and external instruments of perception; even by such a one, the Supreme alone emerges as the utterance "I am" (*aham-asmi*), having ascended to the state of the internal organ (*antaścakra*). Through the dissolution of the distinction between these two, there is the manifestation as "I" (*aham*).

10) Because of the concentration [of consciousness] on the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta) during its arising, and on the second [center], the heart, during its persistence; by remaining there, one will indeed attain the state of fullness. Thus, through the forgetting of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi), one becomes possessed of the reflective awareness "I"—this is the connection. This is the first [stage].
Meditative concentration (dhāraṇā). || 24 ||

Now he states the second [verse]: "The Maruts, whether internal or external, because they follow the pair [or, because they do not turn back from the pair— there is also a reading 'of Bhairava by Bhairavī']..."
In this way, O Bhairavī, the form of Bhairava is manifested as Bhairava.

Because the wind (marut), which consists of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, revolves within and without in the pair of voids— the dvādaśānta and the heart— through its opening and closing (unmeṣa-nimeṣaṇa), O Bhairavī, the body, the physical form, that is to say the essential nature (svarūpa) of Bhairava, the Supreme Self, is indeed manifested and shines forth. || 25 ||
He states the third retention (*dhāraṇā*):
"The power, in the form of the vital breath (*marut*), neither goes out nor enters; it expands" (there is also a reading: "it expands into the form of Bhairava").
By virtue of that non-conceptuality in the middle, he assumes the form of Bhairava.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) which resides in the heart should not depart from its place, nor should it enter elsewhere; rather, let it remain right where it is, motionless in its nature as the non-conceptual form. In this very way, even at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), by being devoid of both movement and stillness within the non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), there occurs the manifestation of the form of Bhairava in that intermediate state.
He defines the fourth concentration (dhāraṇā):
"When [the breath] is either restrained (kumbhita), exhaled (recita), or filled (pūrita), at its conclusion that which is named 'Peace' (śānta) shines forth as peace through Power (śakti). (27)
(p. 11) Having performed *kumbhaka*, *recaka*, or *pūraka* in accordance with the path of the scriptures,
and through the repeated cultivation of those respective practices, one experiences the subsiding of the [mental] momentum, like the stilling of a spinning wheel.

Upon the arising of the state of pure manifestation alone, the nature of both the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā) shines forth indeed. And thus, by the words "he remains with the body maintained through the force of latent impressions (saṃskāra), like the whirling of a potter's wheel," it is shown that manifestation shines forth indeed.
This has been elaborated upon in the *Pratyabhijñā*.
The fulfillment of this reflective awareness of "this," which is otherwise fragmented, is that repose in one's own essential nature; that reflective awareness is this "I am."
By [the words] beginning with "thus," etc. || 27 ||
Now he speaks the fifth [verse]:

"One should contemplate that [light], from its root upwards, appearing as rays, consisting of something subtler than the subtle, subsiding at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], as the arising of Bhairava. (28)

Having meditated upon her— from the root [cakra] up to the heart— as shining with rays like the orbs of the moon and sun, whose nature is luminosity, gradually becoming more and more subtle, and for that very reason subtler than the subtle,
transcending name and form, at the end of the twelve (the *dvādaśānta*), one should contemplate her who is even more extremely subtle than the most subtle.

The ellipsis is that one becomes of the nature of Bhairava through the dissolving away of the form of the object of meditation; the intended meaning is that one should completely abandon that [meditation] as it subsides. || 28 ||

He demonstrates this very point: "Rising in the form of lightning from the sixth [center] through each successive wheel, step by step, until three fist-lengths above; at that end is the Great Arising. (29)

Rising gradually and sequentially from the *kanda* up to the *brahmarandhra*, resembling the form of lightning and possessing a blazing nature, and extending four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) above that, reaching as far as a closed fist— (p.

The Great Arising (*mahodaya*) occurs at the end, reaching as far as the *dvādaśānta*; with the remainder of the three fists, there is indeed the reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) "I am. And so it was sung by the venerable Blessed One:
"I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds."
And so,
for one who fully realizes, "All this is my own manifestation," there is the state of the Great Lord (Maheśatā), even amidst the proliferation of the mental constructs of the Universal Self.
By such [statements], [the same applies] even in the case of recognition (pratyabhijñā). || 29 ||
He speaks of the seventh [verse]:
"The sequence of twelve, properly differentiated by twelve syllables;
having repeatedly released [the self] through the states of gross, subtle, and supreme, then finally..."
The reading is: Śiva. || 30 ||

The twelve wheels— known as the *janma*, *agra*, *mūla*, *kanda*, *nābhi*, *hṛt*, *kaṇṭha*, *tālu*, *bhrūmadhya*, *lalāṭa*, *randhra*, *śakti*, and *vyāpinī*— which are well-known by the names of their twelve locations,
first become manifest through meditation, then begin to vibrate, and finally attain the nature of light.

That which is called "subtle" is designated as "supreme"; and by virtue of that designation, it is Śiva alone who, being all-conquering, shines forth as the illuminator of everything in the ultimate sense. || 30 ||
Now he speaks of the eighth [practice]:
"In that same way, having quickly filled [it] up to the crown of the head by breaking [the flow] with the dam of the eyebrow-contraction."
Having rendered the mind free from conceptual construction, one emerges as the all-pervading source above all.

Having filled [the body] from the wheels of birth and so forth upwards by means of the vital breath (prāṇa) as far as the crown of the head— the limit of twelve (dvādaśānta)— one should break the flow of the mind, like a torrent of water with a dam, by contracting the eyebrows which have been raised upward.

Having rendered that mind free from fickleness and, for that very reason, made it free of conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), one should remain in the supreme space (paramākāśa) above all, even beyond the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta); this is the certainty that one will indeed attain all-pervasiveness.
Now he speaks of the ninth [stage]:
"By means of circles variegated with the feathers of a peacock, one meditates upon the five voids;
for one who meditates thus, there shall be entry into the heart within the unsurpassed void. (32)

Just as the five circles of the sense-faculties appear variegated like peacock feathers— the tail-feathers of a peacock— which possess many colors and diverse forms, so too for one who meditates on this variegated [world] as being nothing but emptiness, there shall be entry into the unsurpassed form of emptiness, the supreme abode, which is the ultimate goal.
Certainty: The sense is that through the certainty that "this is like a city of Gandharvas, like a painting," the realization of ultimate reality (paramārtha) will indeed come to pass. || 32 ||
Now he states the tenth [verse]:
"By this very sequence, wherever one may contemplate [the reading is *cintayet*], she who is merged within herself in the empty wall, in another, or in a vessel, is the bestower of boons. (33)
Thus, for one who meditates in this sequence— whether upon the Supreme, within one’s own self, or elsewhere such as on a wall or in another vessel—
the power of breath (*marucchakti*) becomes spontaneously dissolved once the firmness of one-pointed contemplation is attained.

The meaning is that, through the state of identity with the reflective awareness of the supreme state wherever it may be, there arises the conceit of being one in essence with the nature of "I" (*ahaṃrūpatādātmyatābhimāna*).
And so it is said in the *Śrīspanda* (p.
"Because the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything, since all things arise from it."
Because it is apprehended as being identical with that [object] through the nature of its cognition.
Therefore, in the contemplations of word and meaning, there is no state that is not Śiva;
the enjoyer alone exists everywhere at all times in the form of the object of enjoyment.
Or he whose consciousness perceives the entire world as a play,
constantly seeing it thus and remaining ever-disciplined, is undoubtedly liberated while living.
This has been established by such statements as these. || 33 ||
Regarding the eleventh [day], he says:
"Having placed the mind within the skull, one should remain with eyes closed" (the reading is *tiṣṭhan mīlita*).
Through the gradual firming of the mind, one should perceive the supreme target.
With eyes closed within the hollow of the skull— the cavity between the temples— and with the entire range of internal and external senses withdrawn into the interior of the heart,
one should focus solely on that which is the objective (lakṣya), through the stabilization of the movement of prāṇa, apāna, and the other vital breaths as they set within the *suṣumnā*.
One should perceive it; the meaning is that one sees the supreme light through direct perception, just as one perceives "this is a jar. || 34 ||
He speaks of the twelfth [verse]:

"The Lord shines forth by means of that Goddess who resides in the center of the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī), whose form is like a lotus fiber, and who is meditated upon within the internal void. (35)

The meaning is that when the void-form of Bhairavī— characterized as being subtler than even a spider’s thread— is meditated upon, the self-luminous Lord manifests by the mere act of seeing. And it is said in the *Spanda*:
Then, in that great void where the moon and sun have dissolved,
the deluded one becomes awakened and unobscured, like the state of deep sleep.
This has been demonstrated at length by [the passage] beginning with "ityādi" (and so forth). || 35 ||
Regarding the thirteenth [day], he says:

"When the eye is restrained by the hand with the weapon [of the gaze], and the door is closed by the breaking of the eyebrows, once the *bindu* is seen and has gradually dissolved into its center, there is the supreme state. (36)

The meaning is as follows: for such a yogin whose facial apertures are blocked by both hands and characterized by the gaze [fixed on the brow], through the bursting of the knot at the center of the eyebrows, when the *bindu* is perceived, it gradually dissolves through the intensification of one-pointedness; in that state, there occurs the supreme abiding—the manifestation of Supreme Bhairava. || 36 ||
Regarding the fourteenth [day], he says:

"For one who meditates on the Bindu—shaped like a fine spark of fire produced by internal agitation at the end of the *dhāman*, at the tip of the crest (*śikhā*), and at the end of dissolution in the heart—there is dissolution. (37)
Born from the agitation of the light— that is, from its extreme compression— of that radiance residing in the eye;

or else, born from the agitation— that is, the flickering instability— at the moment when a lamp or other luminous object reaches extinction (*nirvāṇatā*), [one perceives] the *bindu*, which has the form of a subtle spark of fire.

For one who meditates, dissolution occurs within the heart, at the end of the crest-lock (śikhā), at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta), or within the state of dissolved absorption; this constitutes the attainment of oneness with that [reality]. The meaning is that when conceptual construction has dissolved and reached its cessation, there shall be an immersion into the principle of supreme light (paramatejas-tattva). || 38 ||
(p. 16) He speaks of the fifteenth [day]:
"In the unstruck [sound], in the ear that is not a vessel, in the unbroken sound, flowing like a river."
One who is proficient in the Brahman of sound attains the Supreme Brahman. || 38 ||

The attainment of the Supreme Brahman occurs through steadfastness in that Śabda-Brahman which is characterized in ten ways. In what kind of sound? It is not struck—that is, pervaded—by external forms such as blue and so forth; for this very reason, it is "one whose ears are not [confined] to a vessel," because it is distinct from gross sounds and the like. And thus, in "unbroken sound" (*abhagna-śabde*), it is not broken.

The meaning is that one who is firmly established in that sound which is unstruck (anāhata)—the form of the Lord Sound-Brahman (nādabhaṭṭāraka-śabdabrahma) and the swift-flowing river-like [current]—shall attain the state of Brahman. || 38 ||
He describes the sixteenth concentration (dhāraṇā):

"O Bhairavī, by meditating on emptiness at the end of the prolated vowel (*pluta*) following the utterance of the *praṇava* and other [mantras], one attains emptiness through the supreme power (*parā śakti*) which is itself empty. (39)

Because of the short pronunciation of the *praṇava* and the others, followed by their long pronunciation, and then their protracted (*pluta*) pronunciation, there is a pervasive resonance like the crowing of a cock; having mastered that, one transcends emptiness by means of the pronunciation of "emptiness" and "supreme emptiness," taking the state of voidness as the support.
Through the practice of inward-turnedness, the supreme goal is attainable like a bilva fruit in the palm of one's hand; it cannot be otherwise.
Regarding the seventeenth [verse], he says:
"Whosoever among any caste should experience the prior limit [of existence], that person, having become void through the Void, becomes a man whose form is the Void. (40)
First, the training; then, the experience thereof; then, through the grace of the Guru and other means, the ascertainment thereof at the conclusion;
then, the examination of the internal channels (*nāḍī*) and wheels (*cakra*); and finally, having ascertained "Oṃ" through the union of the Void and the Supreme Void, and that [ascertainment]—

Then, within the Supreme Brahman, one attains the state of the void beyond the void; for all this—which has a nature comparable to a city of Gandharvas and so forth—is transcended by the realization that whatever else exists is Brahman. || 40 ||
Regarding the eighteenth [verse], he says:

"When sounds from stringed instruments and the like are long and established in sequence, one whose mind is focused on nothing else shall, at the conclusion, become embodied in the supreme ether. (41)

By the principle of the resonance of sound (*śabdānuraṇana*) and the principle of chewing a medicinal elixir (*pānakacarvaṇa*), the phonemes uttered at each successive moment—such as "de," "va," "da," and "ta"—do not themselves enter into direct experience; rather, it is subsequently that [the whole] is experienced. One wonders, "What is this? What is the purpose here? Yet, because of the proximity of the utterance, the form "Devadatta" arises as something existent.
Thereafter, through the possibility of knowledge arising from another cognition, [one perceives] that "there is a certain Brāhmaṇa named Devadatta";
following that, whether he is eastern, western, southern, or northern;
following that, his habit of studying the Vedas; following that, that "he is the son of Vāmanadatta"; and thereafter...

Furthermore, [the lineage] is indeed perceived as being endowed with its caste, name, and so forth, such that [it is said]: "The brother of Sukhadatta, and thereafter the son of Pṛthūdaryā. Likewise, one whose mind is focused on nothing else amidst the sequences of musical instruments such as the *tantrī* and others, through the state of *laya*, becomes Brahman itself; the sense is that he shall have the supreme ether (*paravyoman*) as his body—he who is proficient in the Śabda-Brahman.
"He attains the supreme Brahman" according to the direction previously stated; or else, "he transcends the Word-Brahman. || 41 ||
(p. 18) Now he states the nineteenth [verse]:
"But by means of the sequence of the gross phonemes of the entire piṇḍa-mantra..."
Through the upward movement of the void that culminates in the crescent moon, the bindu, and the nāda, one becomes Śiva. || 42 ||

The meaning is that by definitively ascertaining— through final resolution— the previously mentioned ninefold self (navātmā) and so forth, or the nine principles (navatattva) and so forth associated with the powers such as Vāmā and the like, starting from the letter 'A' and ending with the letter 'Kṣa', one becomes Śiva through the utterance of the Void (śūnyoccāra). || 42 ||
Now he describes the twentieth dhāraṇā:
"One should simultaneously contemplate the void in all directions within one's own body;
for one whose mind is free from conceptual construction, the entire universe proceeds as the void. (43)

If one should become single-minded with a non-conceptual mind, meditating on space alone in all directions— east and so forth— meditating on emptiness everywhere, thinking that "nothing such as blue or yellow exists," and thus through the meditation that "it is objectless, like [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell," one would become supremely empty; for this reason, of him...

It is merely a conceptual construction such as "void" and so forth. And thus it is stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*: "The true nature of consciousness (cittattva), having abandoned [its unity] through Māyā, appears as if divided—whether in the body, the intellect, the vital breath, or even in the imagined ether."
The reflective awareness "I" as the subject arises from the exclusion of others;
it is indeed a conceptual construction (vikalpa) produced by the manifestation of its opposite.
The sense is that, by such statements as these, that which is the supreme Śiva-tattva— the void beyond the void— is itself what is to be known.
And because, in that very [context]:
The Pralayākalas, however, are agents whose nature is ignorance of [the categories] beginning with Śūnya;
they possess both the karmic impurity (kārmamala) and the māyīya impurity, which is conceptualized.
Thus it has been determined. || 43 ||
Now he describes another dhāraṇā:

"He who meditates simultaneously on the emptiness of the back and the emptiness of the root, from that arises the state beyond conceptualization (nirvikalpa) due to its simultaneous non-conceptual nature. (44)
He who simultaneously meditates upon the emptiness of the back and the emptiness of the root shall become empty-minded through a power that is independent of the body.
One should meditatively cultivate the emptiness of the back, the emptiness of the base, and the emptiness of the heart as stable;
through their simultaneous state of being free from conceptual construction, the arising of non-conceptuality occurs from that.

The reading beginning with these words consists of two verses and is found in the *Uddyota* commentary on the root text (*mūla*). It is inferred that these four intermediate verses were explained by Śrī Śivopādhyāya; furthermore, because they appear redundant, they may not have existed in this manuscript in reality.
Having meditated upon the void above, below, to the south, to the north, and indeed in every direction,
and having reflected through the contemplation that "all this is indeed Brahman," it is no wonder that the Śiva-tattva shines forth like a bilva fruit held in the palm of one's hand. || 44 ||
Regarding another [method], he said:
"In a certain part of the body, one should contemplate emptiness for just a moment.
In the non-conceptual, the non-conceptual [realizes] the nature of the non-conceptual. (nirvikalpe nirvikalpo nirvikalpasvarūpabhāk)
The reading is "vā" || 45 ||
p.

20) Without the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), none of this—which is the locus of the play of consciousness—would appear, for it shines as if painted through its state of solidification. And so it is said in the Siddhāntamuktāvalī:
I see all this as a mere painting; though I am one and partless, I abide as many forms. I am the non-dual self, whose singular nature is infinite bliss.
I remember the world of manifold expansion as being like a woman whose garment has been burnt away.
I experience even a marvel: I behold my body as if it were being plucked away by ants, like a bilva fruit held in the palm of my hand;
and yet, so too do I perceive this life and this very manifestation.
And the attainment of the supreme good is well known to me.
This is what is recorded in such passages as these. Thus, it is established that [the world] is well-known to be unstable, like a city of Gandharvas and the like. || 45 ||
He has also said another [method]:
"O gazelle-eyed one, one should contemplate that every substance contained within the body is pervaded by space;
through that contemplation, it shall become firm. (46)

"All this is pervaded by emptiness, like a snake in a rope, because its nature is established as unreal, like a city of the Gandharvas"— through such meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*), the firm establishment of the conviction that the substances consisting of flesh and so forth located in the body are proven to be emptiness results in the manifestation of light.
The meaning is "it might be so. || 46 ||
Furthermore, in another body, one should contemplate the division of the directions as being merely a wall.
Meditating on nothing within that [state], one does not become a partaker of the object of meditation. || 47 ||

The body, having arisen as connected through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) of the five elements, is gross and perishable by nature, flickering like the tip of an elephant’s ear; thus, there is no stability here—neither was there, nor is there, nor will there ever be.
Likewise, there is no such thing as the division of directions and so forth; this "southern side" is merely an external, adventitious wall.

"Therefore, one should contemplate through the words beginning with 'vottaram' that [the object] is non-existent; and the knower, by means of the certainty that [the subject] is existent, is called a wise man. (47)

He says another [method]: with his senses dissolved in the space of the heart, situated within the hollow of the lotus, with a mind focused on nothing else, O fortunate one, he shall attain supreme fortune. (48)

With the cycle of his external and internal senses bound within the heart-lotus and situated in the center of that lotus-cavity, he—therefore having no other thought—shall attain supreme good fortune; the meaning is that through the cessation of external objects, the internal emergence shall come to pass. || 48 ||
Regarding another [method], he says: "For one of firm intellect, through the dissolution of the mind at the *dvādaśānta* of one's own body from all sides,
the objective reality (*tattvalakṣya*) becomes firmly established and proceeds [to the stage of] *tvagvibhāga*."
"Contemplating it as the foundation," and "it is not to be meditated upon"—this is the reading. || 49 ||

For the yogin of firm intellect, the reality that is the object of focus— characterized by supreme luminosity and having attained a state of intensified one-pointedness— proceeds at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta) due to the dissolution of the mind in the "void beyond void" (śūnyātiśūnya) and the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā).

Alternatively, [it is] in the central abode, namely the *suṣumnā*. This has been clarified in the *Spanda* by such passages as: "Having set [the two breaths] upon the path of the *suṣumnā*, leaving behind the sphere of the cosmic egg," and so forth. (49)
Regarding another [method], he says: "In whatever way and wherever, one should cast the mind into the dvādaśānta;
through days, there will arise a distinct state for one whose mental fluctuations are diminished at every moment. (50)

In this very way, by the method previously described, the manifestation of the extraordinary state of Supreme Bhairava will certainly occur for one whose restlessness has been stilled; such is the meaning. || 50 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:
one should contemplate one's own city as being scorched by the fire of time (kālāgni) arisen from the city of time (kālapura); at the end, a tranquil radiance arises. [From the *Kālapada*]
And there is also the reading: "Then there would be the appearance of peace. || 51 ||

The meaning is that the yogi, having meditated through yoga upon his body being consumed by the fire of time (kālāgni) arising from the big toe of his right foot, perceives himself as the radiant, pure-consciousness (cinmaya) form of the Fire-god (vibhāvasu). || 51 ||
Paparāma said:

"In this very way, having meditated upon the entire world as burnt away through conceptualization, the supreme state of being a man (the realization of the Self) shall arise for that person whose mind is focused on nothing else. (52)

"In the same way," [it is said]; having thus visualized everything— both internal and external— situated within the body as burnt by the flame of Kālāgnirudra arising from the big toe of the right foot, there arises for one whose mind is free of conceptual construction the state of the supreme human goal.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it would become superior to others. || 52 ||

Regarding the other [form], he says: "Having meditated upon the abode of the principles (tattvas) within one's own body or even in the world—principles that are increasingly subtle and most subtle—the supreme [power] is manifested at the end. (53)

Having meditated upon the dissolution— the merging into their respective causes— of the five elements beginning with earth, as well as their transformations such as flesh, bone, and so forth, at the conclusion the Supreme Goddess (Parā Devī) becomes manifest; according to the analogy of the fluid within a peacock's egg, the Supreme [Goddess], who was already situated within all this, appears externally.

The intended meaning is that one should manifest [this]. The essential point here is as follows: through the dissolution of all distinctions and non-distinctions, one who possesses the mantra of supreme grace (parāprasāda) will certainly attain the arising of the Supreme (parodaya). || 53 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:

Having meditated upon the power (śakti) as both plump and weak within the range of the twelve [fingers], and having entered [it] into the heart while meditating, one who is liberated shall attain sovereignty. || 54 ||

First, one should meditate upon the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) as being plump— having attained such plumpness through the consumption of food, drink, and so forth— and then, by means of the teacher’s instruction through practices such as breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), one should contemplate it becoming subtle; having then caused that very energy to enter the heart or the "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānta*), one shall become the form of the independent Supreme Lord (*svatantra-parameśvara*).
Certainty. || 54 ||
Regarding another [method],
he says: one should contemplate everything in its entirety, sequentially, in the form of the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) and so forth.
Through the persistence of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme [states], until finally there is the dissolution of the mind. || 55 ||

The meaning is that by practicing the state of grossness and subtlety regarding that sixfold path— which consists of the levels of existence (*bhuvana*), principles (*tattva*), limited powers (*kalā*), phonemes (*pada*), and mantra-letters (*varṇa*), and which takes the form of the signified and the signifier— one attains the supreme limit through the dissolution of the mind right there within that path. And so it is said in the *Mālinīvijaya*:
It has been taught [in the scriptures] by such statements as, "Śiva exists beyond the temporal paths (adhvan). || 55 ||
Furthermore, others,
having meditated upon the Śaiva reality at the far limits of this entire universe on all sides through the method of the path, attain great exaltation. (56)

Having realized that within the six paths, ending with the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), there is nothing whatsoever that constitutes the essence except for the *śivatattva*—whether generally or specifically—the "Great Awakening" (*mahodaya*) occurs; the meaning is that there arises the manifestation of Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*).
This very [point is as follows]:
Having completely abandoned the six paths and the like, and having conquered the circle of the senses,
he, having accomplished all that was to be done through these means, shines upon the earth like the sun.
This has also been taught in the *Mālinīkalpottara* with the words beginning "ityādinā" (and so forth). || 56 ||
Regarding another [method], he says: "O Great Goddess, one should contemplate this entire universe as having become empty;
and therein the mind becomes absorbed, thereby becoming a vessel for that dissolution. (57)

All this universe, consisting of moving and non-moving beings, is nothing at all; it is like a city of Gandharvas and the like, composed of superimposition, designated as "non-existent" and so forth, devoid of name, form, and the rest, and a dense thicket of *māyā*. That which exists [is thus].
The meaning is that it is characterized as being of the nature of self-luminosity, as the essence, and as the vessel of dissolution. || 57 ||
Regarding another [method], he says: one should cast the gaze into a vessel such as a jar, having abandoned the wall.
Having attained absorption in that at that very moment, through that absorption one becomes identical with it. (58)

The sense is that by setting aside the southern, northern, and other sides within a hollow object such as a jar, and having contemplated the mind as dissolved in the space therein— which is the supreme void beyond the void— one becomes absorbed in the Supreme Brahman and attains Brahman itself. || 58 ||
Regarding another [method], he says: one should cast the gaze upon a place such as one devoid of trees, mountains, or walls;
when the mental state has dissolved, one becomes one whose mental fluctuations have ceased. (59)

Having cast the mere gaze upon a mountain or the like, in a deserted place, in a region of wind, or in a place such as a high peak, because of the absence of any such object of focus, when the mind has dissolved, one becomes one whose all mental fluctuations have ceased. He states another [method]:
When both states are known, one should take recourse in the middle;
having simultaneously abandoned the duality, reality shines forth in the middle.

Having abandoned the essence of that which has fallen into the mass of objects of knowledge—such as "this is a jar," "this is a cloth," "this is a bank"—or else, having realized the state of being a knower within that very midst, someone here...

By asserting that "the knower exists" and thereby establishing non-duality through the multiplicity of the knower, the act of knowing, and the object known, one abandons the conceptualization of division; thus, having attained the state of non-conceptualization—just as in the Mahāvākya "That thou art"—one reaches the state of one-pointedness known as the reality of the subject.
Therefore, it has been well said that through the abandonment of division, one attains one-pointedness. || 60 ||
Then he said another verse as well:
"When existence has been abandoned— [the reading is *bhāve nyakte*, meaning 'when concealed' or 'disappeared']— consciousness, having ceased, does not go to another state of existence."
Then, through that state of being in the center, the meditation blossoms intensely.
When consciousness is focused on a single object and has ceased [from others], it does not go to another entity; nor does it go to a different object.

By abiding in the form of emptiness between those two, meditation blossoms intensely; by way of the analogy of a wondrously blooming flower, the mind reaches a state of extreme expansion—the meaning is that it becomes Brahman itself. || 61 ||

Regarding another [method], he says: one should contemplate the entire body, or indeed the entire world, as consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), simultaneously and with a mind free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). [The reading "the supreme arising of the mind" (*manasaḥ paramodaya*) is also found.]
The movement. || 62 ||

One should contemplate this entire world as the form of consciousness from the feet up to the tips of the hair; and by means of the pervasive wonder of throbbing consciousness, the movement of the mind becomes supreme—that is, its movement takes the form of ultimate excellence—this is the intended meaning.
He states another [method]:
One should contemplate the entire world or one's own body as filled with one's own bliss;
simultaneously, by means of that very nectar of one's own, one becomes composed of supreme bliss.

(27) "Indeed, from bliss alone these beings are born; they proceed toward bliss; they merge back into bliss alone"—with this vision, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done; such is the intended meaning. || 63 ||
Regarding another [point], he says:
Through the friction of the two breaths, whether internally or externally at their limit, the yogi becomes a vessel for the emergence of the consciousness of equanimity. (64)

The sense is that by means of the conjunction of the forms of *prāṇa* and *apāna* within the heart and at the *dvādaśānta*, through their final entry and exit, the awakened yogi— by virtue of the realization of equality— becomes a vessel for the upward ascent, whose sphere of experience consists of the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth, culminating in the secret place (*rahasyasthāna*). And by that...
The meaning is that one shall become a partaker of the supreme accomplishment. || 64 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:
"O gazelle-eyed one, through the practice of *kuhana* (artifice), great bliss arises immediately, by which reality is revealed. (65)

The intended meaning is that through the employment of wondrous illusions (*adbhutamāyā*) and so forth that cause amazement, there shall arise the emergence of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). The remainder [of the sense] is that by means of such reasoning as "I alone am the supreme *haṃsa*," there occurs a pervasion of supreme emergence from the mere touch of an ant. || 65 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:
by the gradual upward movement of the vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*) through the cessation of all streams [of breath]. (Note: *srotonibandhena* is an alternative reading for *sarvasrotonirodhena*).
At the very moment of contact with an ant, supreme bliss expands.

By means of the cessation of the openings of the five sense organs, the secret organ, and the generative organ, [the breath] flows upward in succession from the base (ādhāra) as far as the "twelve-finger space" (dvādaśānta) by way of the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti).

The meaning is that through the contemplation of the thought, "Supreme bliss expands from the mere touch of an ant," one becomes one who delights in the inward-turned state. At the time of experiencing the Self within the *dvādaśānta*, there is [a sensation] like that of a breath moving very slowly, as if of an ant.

The meaning is that from the location of the *mūlādhāra* onwards, up to the location of the *kanda*, there is a tactile sensation; for at that time, yogis examine [the breath], being certain that "having risen from this place, the *prāṇa* has reached such-and-such a place. Through such a cultivation as described, the aforementioned bliss is accomplished. || 66 ||
Regarding another [method], he said: "One should cast the mind, consisting of bliss, into the midst of fire and poison;
or [one should do so] while [the body] is filled only with air, within the bliss of Smara. [End of citation].
Accordingly, the entire reading as thus implied is appropriate. || 67 ||

By means of that retention—by means of easy retention—one should cast the mind even upon fire, poison, or anything very harsh, through the contemplation of ease alone. Or, one should not engage in the retention of desire within the interval between the *prāṇa* and the *apāna*, which consists of the bliss of desire and causes the forgetting of all sense objects; for in the retention of desire, there is the forgetting of all sense objects. Alternatively, [one may practice] when filled with air.

The sense is that even there, although it is devoid of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), there occurs the attainment of non-duality through the dissolution of differentiation. For those who know the ultimate reality (*paramārthavid*) maintain that in the face of suffering—such as fire or poison—the supreme goal is simply the preservation of bliss; likewise, they hold that the experience of bliss with a woman without sexual union is itself the ultimate reality.
It is said: || 67 ||

Regarding another [type of bliss], he says: "That bliss of the reality of Brahman which occurs at the conclusion of the immersion into power (śaktyāveśa), stirred by the union with power (śaktisaṃgama)—that bliss is called 'one's own' (svākyam). (68)

29) It has been stated that one should become filled with bliss by meditating upon that very bliss which is experienced through union with a woman, even in the absence of the woman; and it is further said:
Embraced by his wife, he perceives neither the external nor the internal;
the Śruti provides this illustration, yet the fool considers that state to be the Supreme.
Creation is not born from the male organ, nor from the female organ, nor even from semen;
rather, the Power (Śakti), surging forth with bliss, creates herself by herself.

In accordance with the manner stated in such passages as "ityādi," one should contemplate that bliss which—arising at the conclusion of the immersion into the power of bliss manifested through union with a woman—is a bliss consisting of the mutual reflection between the woman and the man, yet resting solely within one's own self (*svātmamātra*). This is "one's own" (*svakam*), belonging to the Self alone and not derived from anything else; for, according to the teaching beginning with "the union with a woman is merely the cause of manifestation," [the ultimate reality is the Self].
And it has been stated elsewhere: "Enough with excessive detail. (68)
Regarding another [method], he says:
O Mistress of the Gods, through licking, churning, and striking, by the recollection of the fullness of a woman's pleasure, an overflowing of bliss occurs even in the absence of physical power. (69)

The arising of bliss is that very joy which, through the specific acts of kissing, embracing, biting with the teeth, scratching with the nails, and so forth, was previously experienced as the pleasure of women; now, even in the absence of physical capacity, by the mere meditation upon it— or even by meditating merely upon the beauty of the hands and such— it arises as a direct perception that causes one to forget all other objects.
Thus it is established; for the teachers maintain that remembrance of what has been experienced is well known as being nothing other than direct perception. (69)
Regarding another [method], he says:
When great joy has arisen upon seeing a kinsman after a long time, one should meditate on that emerging bliss and, becoming absorbed in it, become one-pointed in mind. (70)
In the same way, when a kinsman, a friend, or someone dear is seen after a long interval,
one grasps the joy that has just arisen; then, through being inwardly absorbed in the contemplation of that [joy], there occurs the emergence of supreme bliss.
The meaning is that one should indeed become rested. And so it is said in the *Spandakārikā*:
"Whether extremely angry or exceedingly joyful, or reflecting 'What shall I do?', or while running—whatever state one enters, therein vibration (*spanda*) is established."
This has been stated by such passages as the above. || 70 ||
He says another [method]:

through the expansion of the bliss of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arising from the joy produced by eating and drinking, one should contemplate the state of fullness; from that, great bliss (*mahānanda*) arises. (71)

This is the intended meaning here: it is established that for one who meditates with a one-pointed mind upon the experience of that bliss whose essence is radiant through the consumption of sweet food and drink and the drinking of milk and other such nourishments, there is the attainment of supreme bliss in the state of being filled with bliss. || 71 ||
Regarding another [type of absorption], he says:

For the yogin whose self is unified with the incomparable bliss of tasting objects such as music, there arises identification with that [object] because the mind has ascended to it through being absorbed in it. (72)

From the tasting—that is, from the relishing—of objects such as songs and the like, or the sweet and subtle sounds of lutes and flutes, there arises a supreme bliss; this very state, characterized by the harmony of rhythm, action, sound, and so forth, is called the arising of the highest supreme bliss, because at that time one forgets all thoughts of the auspicious and the inauspicious. Enough of this elaboration.

And by this, because of the forgetting of the mass of objects to be known, when one abides in the mere existence of the knower and all activity regarding the object of knowledge and the means of knowledge has subsided, the arising of great bliss is certain. || 72 ||
Wherever there is satisfaction of the mind, one should fix the mind right there;
in each such place, the nature of supreme bliss manifests [or: its own nature proceeds forth].
[The reading: || 73 ||

The intended meaning here is this: wherever the mind becomes attached to qualities such as the five senses—thinking "this is auspicious" or "this is inauspicious"—if one comes to rest right there, whether in the auspicious or the inauspicious, one will become composed of the supreme bliss; this is the certainty. At the very moment the mind latches onto whatever is auspicious or inauspicious, [one should remain there].
It is certain that the arising of bliss occurs precisely there, through the forgetting of the reflective awareness of the other. || 73 ||
Regarding another [state], he says: When sleep has not yet arrived and the external field of perception has vanished, that state accessible to the mind shines forth as the supreme Goddess. (74)

The state that emerges in the form of both sleep and wakefulness is called the supreme state (*parāvasthā*), and it is established that this very state is the manifestation of consciousness (*cit*). For instance, that reality which arises at the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking—
Cultivating that state, one directly attains imperishable bliss.
This has been established by such passages as the above. || 74 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:
When the sky is variegated by the brilliance of the sun, lamps, and so forth, one should fix the gaze right there; therein, the form of one's own self shines forth. (75)
In the specific upper and lower locations belonging to the great sky, which is variegated by the light of the sun's rays during the day and by the moonlight at night.

For one who practices the binding of the gaze with an undistracted mind— whether in a room whose space is pervaded by the light of a lamp situated in a corner of the house, or in the presence of a painting— the manifestation of one's own essential nature occurs through its unification with the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*); and the fruit of this is the knowledge of the fourteen worlds.
And the superknowledge of the supreme mental disposition of the array of Tārās arises. || 75 ||
He says that another [attainment] occurs at the time of the gaze of Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhanā, Bhairavī, Lelihānā,
and Khecarī; this is the supreme pervasion (*parā vyāptiḥ*)— [the reading is *parāvāptiḥ*].
It shines forth. || 76 ||

The sense is that, as she perceives the universe as a mere skeleton devoid of movement, like a corpse— whether with her power of vision distracted by anger, or with it one-pointedly intent on devouring, or extended far for the sake of beholding the sky— at the moment of seeing, a supreme pervasiveness shines forth. || 76 ||
Regarding another [method], he said:
"On a soft seat, having placed one's hands and feet without support using only one buttock, through that practice, the supreme, full realization shall arise. (77)

The essential meaning is as follows: just as it occurs when there is no support, so too, having placed the feet and hands [in such a way], while being conscious of all the limbs in their respective parts and in their entirety, the intellect—having shed the qualities of *tamas* and *rajas*—becomes composed of *sattva*. On a soft seat, that is, a gentle seat, with one hip on a hard seat.
For it is established that by sitting in such a way, there arises an obstruction such as being hunchbacked or tall, which leads to instability in meditative absorption (samādhi). || 77 ||
Regarding another [method],
he said: "Having sat upon the seat, one should properly bend both arms [the reading 'kṛtvārthakuñcitau' is understood as 'having bent them for the purpose']."
[The reading:
"In the space of the armpit, casting [the breath] aside, one attains peace through absorption in that. || 79 ||
Sitting on a seat and drawing the arms back into the space between the armpits, one attains tranquility through absorption in that [state].
Regarding another [method], he says:
having fixed the gaze steadily upon a gross object...
Having made the mind supportless in no long time, one shall go to Śiva.

By means of the opening and closing of the eyes, one should fix the gaze that has become motionless for that very reason; having rendered the mind supportless and not thinking of anything at all, one should attain Śiva—the state of unity with the Supreme Self. This is the intended meaning.
He states another [method]:
Having placed his consciousness between [the teeth] with the tongue in the middle and the mouth wide open,
and pronouncing the syllable "Ha" mentally, he then dissolves into the state of peace.

The meaning is that when the mouth is opened such that the tongue is positioned exactly in the middle, one should fix the intellect within that [mouth] and, uttering the sound "ha" by means of the mind alone, the tranquil self shines forth. || 81 ||
Regarding another [method], he said:
"Remaining on a seat or in a bed, one should contemplate [it] as being without support; contemplating one's own body..."
The reading is *kṣaṇāt kṣīṇāśayaḥ*.
Following the verse beginning with *līnaṃ mūrdhni* (84), Utpaladeva’s commentary (*u0 mū0*) states:
"Beholding the pure sky, having fixed one's gaze without interruption."
O Goddess, at that very moment, one whose self is thus steadied shall attain the form of Bhairava.
[Thus there is an additional verse:
When one's own body and mind have perished, the latent tendencies of the elements (bhūtāśaya) would vanish in an instant. (82)

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: by contemplating that there is no seat within the body because even the body is without support, and by remaining in a state of reclining while thinking "I am not the body" and "the body is not mine," there arises no conceptualization of a support or the like for that which is itself the common substratum. Through such contemplation, when the mind is exhausted and the mass of objects of knowledge has dissolved, one becomes "one whose latent tendencies have perished" (bhūtāśaya) and "one who has realized the true nature of reality" (bhūtasiddhārtha). || 82 ||
Regarding another [method], he said:
"O Goddess, when one is seated on a movable seat, or by the gentle movement of the body, once the state of the mind has become tranquil, one shall attain the Divine Current (divyaugha). (83)

While slowly moving the body on a moving vehicle such as a horse, and when the mental state has become tranquil, one shall attain—that is, reach—the essence of that splendor by uniting with the flood, the multitude, of the divine worlds and of the supreme yogis; such is the intended meaning. || 83 ||
Regarding another [method], he says: One should contemplate the entire void at the crown of the head as being Bhairava;
one should enter that entire reality of light (tejastattva) which has the form of Bhairava. (84)
The meaning is that for one who contemplates that everything— whether withdrawn, conjoined, or all else such as blue, yellow, and so forth— is composed of Śiva, Brahman shines forth. || 84 ||

Regarding another [objection], he says: "Having known what? [The reading 'having known that something has been known' (kiṃcijjñātamiti jñātvā) and 'infinite' (ananta) also occurs. External light again brings about darkness, which gives rise to duality."
Having meditated upon the form of Bhairava, which is the beginning of all things and which sustains infinite light, [one becomes] the bearer of infinite radiance. (85)
Having first meditated on the differentiated nature [of reality], thinking "Is it a post or a person?", and then having meditated on all this—

the external light such as the moon and sun, and then the darkness— as being the form of Bhairava, one becomes Bhairava, who consists of infinite light due to the dissolution of multiplicity. || 85 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:
"In this very way, during the long night of the dark fortnight, one should contemplate the form of Bhairava as being shrouded in darkness. [The reading "bhāvayan rūpam" is also found.]
He will attain form. || 86 ||
A night shrouded by clouds is a difficult night; within that night, which takes the form of *andhatāmisra*, *mahātāmisra*, and *tāmisra*,

one should contemplate that which is dark as the color of time (*kālaśyāmala*), possessing a terrifying form, sealed with the Bhairava-mudrā, marked by the Bhairava-mudrā, and invisible due to its fearfulness— by contemplating that form, one attains imperishable bliss.
Because it produces wonder. || 86 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:

"In the same way, having closed the eyes at the beginning and so forth, one should visualize the form of Bhairava as black before oneself; becoming absorbed in that, one should contemplate it. [Bhāvayaṃstanmaya iti]
[The reading] would be as follows: || 87 ||

Closing his own eyes, even though it was not the night of the dark fortnight, he perceived a black appearance in the form of darkness and, struck with wonder, thought: "What is this? This very thing is the Bhairava-form; [it appears] in this form."
There should be a state of identification with that. || 87 ||

Regarding another [objection], he says: "Because of the contradiction and because of cessation at the beginning of whichever sense-faculty [or 'of any sense-faculty whatsoever'— the reading there is *tatraivātmeti*]."
For one who has entered the non-dual void, the Self shines forth at that very moment. || 88 ||
The sense is that, because external agency has ceased due to the absence of ignorance, and because of the resulting contradiction and the conjunction of opposites,

as well as through cessation and the act of ceasing, one enters into the non-dual— which is devoid of duality and empty— and thus, by resorting to the inward-turned state, the Self shines forth. || 88 ||
Regarding another [mantra], he said:
"O Goddess, for one who recites the syllable *a* without the nasal drop (*bindu*) or the visarga, a great flood of knowledge, the Supreme Lord himself, suddenly arises. (89)

In the case of "am" and "aḥ," having abandoned the bindu and visarga, for one who remains in *kumbhaka* (retention) and recites only "a" alone, the flood of knowledge (*jñānaugha*) of the Supreme Lord arises. The meaning is that by abandoning all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) through freedom from them, that which remains becomes precisely that—just as in the teaching "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*). || 89 ||
Regarding another [method], he says: At the end of a vowel accompanied by *visarga*, place the consciousness upon the *visarga* (the reading is *visargāntam*).
With a mind that is without support, one should touch the eternal Brahman. (90)

Furthermore, in this context, having likewise discarded the letter *a*, what remains in the case of *am* and in the case of *aḥ* are the bindu and visarga (*ḥ*); because these two are inexpressible, the supreme state is attained therein.
Thus, it is established that [this] is liberation (nirvṛti). || 90 ||
Regarding another [method], he said:
One should meditate upon one's own self as having the form of space, unenveloped by the directions;
then the consciousness-power (citi-śakti), being without support, reveals its own true nature. 91.
"I alone am the supreme *haṃsa*, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest.

Having thus made one's own self to be of the nature of space, and likewise having freed it from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the directions, blue, yellow, and so forth, the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), being without support, [abides in] its own true form.
The intended meaning is that one should show [it]. || 91 ||
Regarding another [method], he says: First, one should pierce some part [of the body] with a sharp needle or similar instrument;
then, consciousness becomes joined to that very spot—this is the stainless state of Bhairavī. (92)
Or, that power of endurance which arises from withstanding the piercing of the body with sharp needles and the like, or by means of fire, is itself designated as "consciousness" (cetanā). It is said:
"This [Self] is neither to be cut, nor to be burned, nor to be moistened, nor to be dried."
The meaning is that, by recollecting such words of the Blessed One, one attains similarity in form with Bhairava. || 92 ||
Regarding another [objection], he says: "If one were to contemplate that there is no internal mental construction (antahkṛti) such as the mind and so forth within me" [the reading is *bhāvayet*].
Even in the absence of conceptual constructions, one would be liberated from conceptual constructions. || 93 ||

(38) "The group of internal organs, beginning with the mind (*citta*), does not exist within me; even if it seems to exist, it truly does not exist. Thus, through the cessation of external objects, one becomes firmly established in this contemplation, and consequently, by the absence of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
The meaning is that, being abandoned by and freed from conceptual constructions through the state of non-conceptuality, one becomes pure consciousness. || 93 ||
He speaks of another [power], called Māyā, which is the deluder; the function (*kalana*) of Kalā is established.
Thus, by perceiving the attributes of the principles (*tattva*s) beginning with this, one should not become separate from them. [The reading "kalayannāpṛthak" is understood as "kalayan na pṛthak"].
[The reading: || 94 ||

This illusion is called "the deluder," and it consists of the differentiation of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth; by thus differentiating the *kalā* (limited agency), the person (*puruṣa*) becomes distinct. The meaning is that he would then be designated as "transcending all" and "immovable" (*kūṭastha*). || 94 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:
one should immediately bring to rest a desire as soon as it has arisen;
for it dissolves right back into that very source from which it originated. (95)
Having thus reflected with inward focus, one should bring to rest— that is, lead to pacification— right there within that [mind] from which [the thoughts] have arisen as agitation of the mind,
just as waves [subside] in waters or bubbles in the ocean.
In this manner, by relying on unity and pacifying all that [duality], one then attains Brahman oneself. || 95 ||
Regarding another [view], he says: "When neither desire nor knowledge has arisen in me, who indeed am I then?
In reality, I am of such a nature; one should become absorbed in that and have the mind fixed on it. (96)

39) Even when a multitude of will, knowledge, action, and so forth has arisen—such as "I do" or "I go"—and even though such cognition has arisen, in reality I am only the nature of the Self (*ahaṃsvarūpa*); when that [cognition] has dissolved, I am absorbed in that [Self].
"So it should be," say the teachers. And thus, in the *Spanda*:

"The outpourings of the vibration of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, by virtue of resting upon the universal vibration, constantly attain their own existence and do not become obstacles for the knower."
But these [beings] of unawakened intellect, intent on concealing their own true state,
cast others onto the terrible path of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross.
Therefore, one who is constantly diligent in discerning the reality of Spanda attains his own true nature even while awake, without delay.
This has been very clearly established by such statements as these. || 96 ||

Regarding another [method], he says: "When desire or knowledge has arisen, one should fix the mind with the thought 'this is the Self,' being single-minded; from that comes the vision of the true nature of reality. (97)

The meaning is that when desire has just arisen, or when knowledge has just arisen, if one possesses a firm contemplation of the nature of one's own self regarding everything, then the vision of the reality of the Self will certainly occur for one whose mind is not distracted by anything else; this is certain because of the practice of [the realization] "All this, indeed, is Brahman. || 97 ||
Regarding another [view], he says:
"Knowledge would be signless (*nirnimitta*), without support (*nirādhāra*), and of the nature of delusion (*bhramātmaka*).
In reality, for no one is it thus; O Dear One, Śiva is not like that. (98)

Like the [perception] "this is silver" in the case of mother-of-pearl, the entire range of the visible world is by its very nature mere delusion, being without cause; and for this very reason, it is without foundation and devoid of any substratum.

The sense is that because everything is indeed pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), since there is nothing else apart from consciousness, one becomes Śiva himself through the firmness of such contemplation. || 98 ||
Regarding another [point], he says:
"The attributes of consciousness (ciddharma) exist in all bodies; there is no distinction anywhere.
Therefore, a person who has conquered worldly existence should contemplate everything as being composed of that [consciousness]. (99)

In forms such as gods, asuras, humans, animals, and both stationary and moving beings, the attributes of consciousness (ciddharma) exist in common; there is no distinction anywhere therein.
