It is only the body and its adjuncts that possess distinction, but not consciousness. Contemplating thus, and through the firmness of the experience that "consciousness alone unfolds everywhere," one who contemplates "I am That" becomes a conqueror of worldly existence.
A person becomes one who has crossed over the difficult-to-traverse cycle of existence. || 99 ||
Regarding another [verse], he said:
"In the sphere of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, having made the intellect motionless, that very reality remains. (100)

Having made the intellect one-pointed regarding [the states] beginning with desire and anger and ending with envy, and having rendered it motionless by not perceiving modifications, that very reality—pure consciousness—remains; this is the remainder. || 100 ||
Another says: "The entire universe is composed of illusion (indrajāla), or it is like a painted scene laid out;
for one who wanders or meditates, everything [appears as such]. (Note: The reading is *bhramato dhyāyataḥ*, though *bhramadvā dhyāyataḥ* is also a variant.)
And for one who sees [this], there arises happiness. || 101 ||
Thus, having contemplated this entire universe as being like a magical illusion through a mind certain by means of the reasoning of the experience of knowledge,
one wanders through and contemplates all this while ascending upon one's own spontaneous vibration (*svaspanda*).
Even while seeing, one becomes possessed of inexhaustible happiness—the meaning is that by seeing "all this is Brahman," one is liberated. || 101 ||
Another says:
"One should not cast the mind into suffering, nor should one cast it into pleasure.
O Bhairavī, what reality remains for those who meditate in the middle? (102)

The meaning is that when one has realized all this— whether it be the manifestation of pleasure, pain, and so forth, or indeed everything as either pleasure or pain— and meditates upon it with one-pointed concentration, O Bhairavī, the arising of Bhairava occurs in the midst of that.

Regarding another [method], he says: Having abandoned attachment to one's own body, one should contemplate "I am everything" with a firm mind and vision; by not looking at anything else, one becomes happy. (103)

Having abandoned the state of being a subject limited to one's own body—by means of the realization "I am not the body," and so forth—one subsequently contemplates that "all this is indeed myself," and thus remains happy everywhere and at all times. (103)

Regarding another [objection], he says: "That consciousness, desire, and so forth which exist within me in relation to a jar and the like, have not arisen as omnipresent. By meditating thus—"I am omnipresent"—[one becomes] all-pervading. [That is, by meditating: "I am everywhere."]
[The reading: || 104 ||

(42) That which is always, everywhere, and in all states perceived by the cognition of jars and so forth as "this is a jar," and the desire within that [cognition] such as "I shall act thus," all of that, even though it has arisen, [is non-existent].
The sense is that by contemplating how nothing at all exists because of its lack of substantiality (niḥsāratva), one should become of the nature of light (prakāśasvarūpa) everywhere. || 104 ||
Regarding another [point], he says: "The cognition of the apprehended and the apprehender is common to all embodied beings;
however, this is the distinction for yogis: attentiveness toward that connection."

The conventional usage among all embodied beings, from Sadāśiva down to the smallest insect—expressed as "this is the object" and "this is the subject"—is indeed common to all; for what one person knows, another also knows, and thus it is universal. However, this is the specific distinction for yogins regarding their connection [to that reality]: [The verse continues: "Even though the object is common to all, the yogin perceives it through his own particularity. (3.2.10) The meaning is as follows: although the object is common to all, the yogin perceives it through his own particularity (*viśeṣa*). This is because he has attained mastery over the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) by means of the supreme *sāmarasya* (state of aesthetic/ontological equilibrium). Therefore, even though the object is common, the yogin perceives it as if it were unique to himself. Consequently, the yogin’s experience is not merely common; rather, it is characterized by a particularity that distinguishes him from others. The meaning is that in the determination of the essential nature of the grasped and the grasper, there is the non-forgetting of the nature of the grasper; [this is expressed as] "I am the rememberer," who is always of the nature of light, while everything else—the object of knowledge—is said to be impermanent and unreal. || 105 ||
Regarding another [method], he says: One should experience consciousness even in the body of another;
having abandoned attachment to one's own body, one becomes all-pervasive within days. (106)

Contemplating that this entire world is his very body, he should abandon the mere perception of duality and, relinquishing all regard for his own individual body, [realize]: "This is not my body; it is not something other than the [universal] Self.
The meaning is that by means of this firm contemplation (*dṛḍhabhāvanā*) upon one’s own self-consciousness alone within all that is other, he shall become pervasive in those very days. || 106 ||
He spoke another [verse]:
"O gazelle-eyed one, having made the mind supportless, one should not conceptualize through conceptualization; in that state of both the individual self and the supreme self, one is Bhairava. (107)
All this, which consists of the superimposition of one's own individual nature—such as "Is it a post or a person?"—must be abandoned.

Having attained steadfastness in the identity of one's own self with the Supreme Self, and having reached or realized absorption in the Supreme Self, the meaning is that one becomes the Supreme Self itself in the form of Bhairava. || 107 ||
The Omniscient One has said another [verse]: "The Supreme Lord is all-knowing, the creator of all, and all-pervading;
I am He alone, a follower of the Śaiva dharma. Through such firm conviction, one becomes Śiva. (108)

"I am he, and he is indeed I; this Śaiva dharma belongs to Śiva, for all my sovereignty and other qualities belong to him. By means of this firm contemplation, one attains identity with Paramaśiva. || 108 ||
Regarding another [view], he says:

"Just as the waves belong to the water, the flickering flames to the fire, and the radiance to the sun, so too these various manifestations of the universe are merely differentiated forms of myself, Bhairava. (109)

Just as waves arise from water alone, or flames from fire, or radiance from the sun, so too these universal manifestations of Bhairava—such as going and coming, eating, offering oblations, giving, stretching out, departing, and so forth—exist; one should contemplate them in this way. This is the implied meaning. || 109 ||
Another says:
"Having wandered and wandered through bodies on the earth, quickly [with the body—this is the reading]," p. 44.
From the falling away [of the breath], through the cessation of the power of agitation, the supreme state arises. (110)
The meaning is that, just like the act of circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇakriyā*), after undergoing thousands of births and transitions through various wombs—
such as those of humans, gods, asuras, and animals— a supreme state manifests for one whose sorrow has been exhausted through the glance of a true guru (*sadguru*). It is exactly so.
"When agitation dissolves, then the supreme state arises"—this and more is established in the *Spanda* [Kārikās], verse 9u. || 110 ||
Regarding another [method],
he says: "Or else, by means of the powers within the supports, through meditation, and by the dissolution of the mind" (the reading "by power, ignorance, and the mind" is also found).
Following verse 112, the oral tradition (u0 mū0) states:
"Having contracted the ears, and likewise during the downward expulsion [of breath], while meditating on the 'syllable-less Mahala,' one should enter the eternal Brahman. (114)
[Thus there is an additional verse: "Or: At the end of the agitation caused by the immersion of the arisen power, [one attains] the body of Bhairava. (111)

The meaning is that because objects cannot be known, or due to the absence of cognition and so forth, there occurs a dissolution of the mind; through that, a disturbance of immersion arises within the supportless power (*anāśrita-śakti*), at the end of which the form of Bhairava indeed manifests. || 111 ||
He spoke another tradition: "O blessed lady, listen; I shall tell you correctly.
Kaivalya arises immediately when the eyes are merely fixed in a steady gaze. (112)

The meaning is that for the yogin— who has forgotten this entire world consisting of both difference and non-difference and has fixed his gaze upon the inner self— the light of consciousness (*cittaprakāśa*) will surely arise wherever he may be.

In all these instructions, both those already stated and those yet to be stated, the intended goal is the practice of one-pointedness of mind through the discernment of pure consciousness alone. || 112 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:

By gazing into a great pit such as a well—[the reading "standing above" (sthitvopari) is also found]—the mind of one whose intellect is free from conceptual construction clearly attains immediate and perfect absorption into the state of *citta-laya*. (113)

If it flashes forth in this way, there is nothing here whatsoever that falls within the category of the knowable or unknowable, such as blue, yellow, and so on; rather, the intended meaning is that only the most terrible Bhairava body, appearing here, shines forth. || 113 ||
Regarding another [aspect], he says: "O Beloved, wherever the mind goes—whether externally or internally—therein lies the state of Śiva; because of its all-pervasiveness, where could it go? (114)
Wherever the mind goes— naturally restless and unstable— one should restrain it from that very place and bring it under control within the Self alone.

Through such words spoken from the mouth of the Blessed One, because of the certainty that "wherever the mind goes toward blue, yellow, and so forth, as its inner self, there in each instance is the state of Śiva," the manifestation of Bhairava arises. And thus, in the *Śrīspanda* (p.
Because the individual soul consists of everything, since it arises from all states of being,
and because it attains identity with them through the nature of their perception.
Therefore, in the contemplations of word and meaning, there is no state that is not Śiva;
the enjoyer alone is always and everywhere established in the form of the object of enjoyment.

"Or he whose consciousness perceives the entire world as a play, constantly seeing thus and remaining ever-yoked, is undoubtedly liberated while living. This and more has been established [in the text]. 114.
Regarding another [aspect], he says:

"Wherever consciousness of the All-pervasive One is manifested through the path of the senses, because that [consciousness] has only that [object] as its substrate, there arises the state of being the full Self through the dissolution of the intellect. (115)

Wherever consciousness of the All-pervasive Lord is manifested through meditation on the state of Śiva— and because that [consciousness] has as its sole attribute the nature of those [limited] categories, and because its essential nature is pure consciousness alone— it attains a state of fullness through resting in dissolution within Cit (the Absolute Consciousness); thus, "I alone am the universe."

The meaning is that by being filled with great consciousness, one attains the state of realized reality, just as water becomes solidified like ice or ghee; for [the soul] has attained the nature of water. || 115 ||

Regarding another [state], he says: at the end of hunger and so forth, in fear, in grief, or in the depths of fleeing from battle— [there is also the reading "the state consisting of pure being" (sattāmayī daśā)].
In curiosity, at the end of hunger and other such states, the reality of Brahman is near.
Whether one is extremely angry or exceedingly joyful, or when pondering "What shall I do?", or while running—whatever step one takes, therein vibration is established. (22) p.

The meaning is that by reflecting upon the form of Bhairava as indicated in the aforementioned direction of the *Spanda* [Kārikās], and having contemplated it during hunger and other such states through the reasoning heard from the mouth of the Guru, one certainly becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtya*).
This has been determined in detail in the *Tantrāloka* and other works; therefore, it should be understood from those very sources. For fear of excessive length, it is not treated here.
This has been illustrated by way of a mere indication of its direction. || 116 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:
while objects are being remembered, one should cause the mind to abandon the perceived location;
then, having made one's own body supportless, it proceeds forth (the reading *prasarati* is supported by the variant *prasaratīti*).
The Lord. || 117 ||

Through the power of recollection and so forth, when the object is perceived, one should withdraw the mind from the power of sensory experience which resides in its own substratum, and take it up with one-pointed concentration; one should then cause one's own body to shine forth as supportless and unattached, like a snake that has cast off its skin.
Thereafter, the Lord manifests of His own accord—this is the certainty. The underlying meaning here is as follows:
It is established that, as in a string, the expansion of consciousness is strung together through experience and recollection like a cluster of gems;
therefore, one should meditate upon that very [consciousness]—this is the remainder of the sense. || 117 ||
Regarding another [method], he said: "Having slowly fixed the gaze upon some object, one should withdraw it;
O Goddess, that knowledge together with the mind becomes the abode of emptiness. (118)

Having fixed one's gaze upon something and placed in the mind the experience of that object as "this is a jar," accompanied by its latent impression (*vāsanā*), one whose intellect has become void should remain; the meaning is that he attains Brahman. || 118 ||
He spoke of another:
"The kind of mind that arises in one who is detached due to the intensity of devotion—that is the power of Śaṅkara; one should constantly cultivate it, for through it one becomes Śiva. (119)

The kind of realization that arises in the mind of one who is detached through the excellence of devotion and whose mind is tranquil, by means of the concentration of the mind upon the Mind— that is proclaimed as the Śāṅkarī Śakti; one should meditate upon that very power so that one may become identical with it.

Regarding another [method], he says: When one object is being experienced, emptiness gradually arises with respect to all objects. By meditating on that very [emptiness] with the mind, even though the mind is diverse (or, according to another reading, "even though it is known"), it becomes tranquil.

This is the intended meaning here: when one object is known as being of the nature of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*), there arises the cognition of non-existence regarding other objects; for this would result in the entire world attaining a single uniform nature. Therefore, since even a single object would—by virtue of its conscious essence—result in possessing the nature of everything, [the opponent concludes] that all objects of knowledge must be empty.
Having meditated with such diversity, one becomes liberated through the absence of conceptualization and discursive thought; this is the certainty. || 120 ||
Regarding another [view], he says: That purity which is taught by those who know only a little is not true purity in the vision of Śambhu;
for one is neither pure nor impure. Therefore, one should become Śiva, free from conceptual construction. (121)
"Having thoroughly performed the washing of the feet, one should then drink the pure water three times"—
by such statements, purification is prescribed; yet that very purification does not apply to one who is established in non-conceptual samādhi.
"Neither pure nor impure, because there would otherwise be a loss of non-differentiation"—this is the ultimate ultimate truth. And thus:
49) "Whether one casts off the body in Kāśī or in the house of an outcaste..."
The knower of that incurs no blemish, just as gold situated in mud remains untainted.
This and more is recorded in the Smṛti. || 121 ||
Regarding another [view], he says: "The state of Bhairava pervades everywhere; it is the object even within common universals (*sāmānya*).
Since there is nothing else apart from that, this is the non-dual realization. (122)
"Just as the manifold variety of cities, villages, and so forth appears in the reflection of a mirror as something undivided,
yet appearing as if divided from one another and even from the mirror itself" (Pañcārthasāra 12)—
by such passages, it is shown that the state of Bhairava is manifest everywhere and at all times within all objects, both external and internal.

And since there is nothing whatsoever apart from that, through the attainment of awakening, the state that transcends duality would be non-dual knowledge; for if it were separate from that, it would follow that it lacks the quality of being manifest. || 122 ||
Regarding another [quality], he said:
"He who is equal toward enemy and friend, and equal in honor and dishonor, should become happy by knowing this through the perfection of Brahman. (123)
And as it was sung by the Blessed Lord: "The wise look with an equal eye upon a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste."
And likewise, in the illustration of the sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*) and others: "Whether upon a snake, or a necklace, or upon a bed of flowers, or on a stone slab..."

When will my days pass in a sacred forest, where I look with equal vision upon a jewel or a clod of earth, a powerful enemy or a friend, a blade of grass or a woman, while crying out, "Shiva! Shiva! Shiva!"?
Furthermore, in the Siddhāntamuktāvalī,
it is said: "By him, a bath was taken in the waters of all sacred fords, the entire earth was gifted away,
a thousand sacrifices were performed, and all the gods were fully gratified."
He has rescued his own ancestors from saṃsāra; even he who is worthy of worship by the three worlds would find his mind attaining stability for even a moment in the contemplation of Brahman.
Thus, the sense is that by realizing that the entire manifold of the universe is indeed composed of consciousness alone—the radiance of will, knowledge, and action—one becomes happy. || 123 ||
This being so, another says:
"One should never cultivate hatred anywhere, nor should one ever cultivate passion.
When liberated from both passion and hatred, Brahman flows forth in the middle. (124)
The sense is that there is aversion toward snakes and the like, and attachment toward necklaces and the like; when one attains a nature free from these, one becomes Brahman. || 124 ||
Regarding another [aspect], he says:

That which is unknowable, that which is ungraspable, that which is empty, and that which is the realization of non-existence—all that should be contemplated as Bhairava; at its conclusion, the emergence of pure consciousness occurs. (125)
For that bliss of Brahman from which words turn back, together with the mind, failing to reach it— the knower of that does not fear anything whatsoever.
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire.
Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined.
"Verily, from bliss these beings are born;
by bliss, once born, they live; unto bliss they pass and merge.
By such passages as this, it is established that all this is indeed Brahman alone—this being so everywhere through the power of firm realization.
One who possesses the awakening to the true nature of Bhairava becomes Bhairava himself—the meaning is that he attains Brahman.

Regarding another [method], he says: Having fixed the mind on the external space—which is eternal, supportless, empty, all-pervading, and devoid of mental construction—one should enter into the spaceless. (126)
Thus, the sense is that by means of the excellence of the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on emptiness directed precisely toward external space— which is experienced as being eternal and all-pervading—
and through the excellence of that practice, one enters into that very abode which has become the "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyātiśūnya*). || 126 ||
Regarding another [method], he says:
"Wherever the mind goes, at that very moment, by abandoning each of those through non-abiding, one then becomes waveless. (127)

The meaning is that, by means of the mind in the form of non-conceptual self-awareness, having abandoned all of that at that very moment through the method of attaining the objectless, one becomes possessed of the nature of Supreme Bhairava. || 127 ||
Regarding another [etymology], he says:
because he makes everything resound with fear, he is "all-pervading" (bhairava), encompassing the entire universe; thus, Śiva is so called due to the continuous utterance of the word "Bhairava. (128)
This entire universe, out of fear, either cries out, reflects, or else protects and preserves itself.

Because of the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) "I am" toward the entire mass of knowable objects—whether blue or non-blue, pleasure or pain—and because of the attainment of firmness through the experience "I am everywhere, both within and without," one becomes Śiva. And thus, it is not so.
This has been handed down in the tradition in such passages as, "That state is not auspicious," and so forth. || 128 ||
Regarding another [type of meditation], he says:
Through the cessation of the tendency toward notions such as "I," "mine," and "my," the mind, being without a support, becomes tranquil through the impulsion of that meditation. (129)

The meaning is that by making the mind supportless amidst such occurrences as "I am this," "this is mine," and "by me," and by being impelled through the practice of meditating on the thought "this is not, there is nothing manifold," one attains the power of the self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśa*); thus, becoming tranquil, with dualities stilled, one becomes one who has attained supreme liberation (*paranirvāṇa*).
Another says: He is eternal, all-pervasive, without support, omnipresent, and the sovereign of all;
he meditates upon words every moment in accordance with their intended meanings. (130)
The meaning is that by meditating at every moment in this way— “Śiva alone is omnipresent, omniscient, and everywhere”—
one indeed becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done through the perception of the nature of things (padārthadṛṣṭi), in accordance with the subject matter at hand.
The sense is that one would possess the nature of liberation precisely in the realization "I know" and "I act. And so it is stated in the *Spanda*:

"The outpourings of the vibration of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, by virtue of resting upon the universal vibration, constantly attain their own existence and do not constitute obstacles for the Knower. (19)
But these [beings] of unawakened intellect, striving to conceal their own true state, cast others onto the terrible path of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross. (20)
Therefore, one who is constantly engaged in the discernment of the reality of Spanda attains his own true nature even while awake, without delay.
This has been determined by such [statements] as these. || 130 ||
Regarding another [objection], he says: "All this is established as unreal, appearing like a magical illusion (indrajāla).
What is the reality of a magical illusion? By [reflecting on] this, one attains tranquility through firmness. (131)

The meaning is that through the realization—"This is not reality; it is essence-less, like a magical illusion"—and by means of the firm cultivation of the thought that "all this is indeed equal to a magical illusion, and that which should be designated as the supreme existent reality is the principle of the knower," the knower of reality attains the state of liberation (nirvāṇa). || 131 ||
Another says: Where is there knowledge or where is there action for the self that is devoid of modification?
Since external objects depend upon knowledge, this world is therefore empty. (132)
p.
54) Since there is no connection with powers such as knowledge and action, how could there be any conceptualization of objects of knowledge and so forth? It is not from any source whatsoever.
Therefore, the meaning is that this world appears as nothing other than non-conceptual, for it is itself of a non-conceptual nature. And thus:
In the *Mālinīvijaya*,
that power of the Creator of the universe which is said to be inherent [in Him],
O Goddess, assumes the nature of His will when He desires to emit [the world].
Listen to how even that which is single attains multiplicity:
it should be known with perfect certainty that "it is thus" and not otherwise.
When she makes known [the will] here in this world, saying "let all this be so," and is oriented toward action, she is called the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
At that very moment, the action is considered to be performed in such and such a manner;
thus, it is of two forms, and furthermore, manifold through its various divisions.
By the power of the limiting adjunct of objects, the Sovereign Lady becomes like a wish-fulfilling gem;
having first entered therein into the state of the Mothers, she then manifests in various forms.
This meaning has been elucidated by such passages as: "The Mālinī [is divided] in two ways, in nine ways, and in fifty ways. (132)
Regarding another [view], he says:
"For me there is neither bondage nor liberation; these are merely terrors for the fool.
This is a reflection of the intellect, like that of the sun in waters. (133)
"By virtue of being possessed by *māyā*, the person whose consciousness is defiled becomes a bound soul (*paśu*).
This point, established by such passages, is very clearly elucidated in the *Paramārthasāra*. Furthermore, in that same work, it is said:
"Just as the reflection of the moon moves when the water moves, and remains still when [the water] is still..."
"Thus, this Great Lord, the Self, [is present] within the group consisting of the body, the instruments, and the worlds" (Pañcārthabhāṣya 7).
By such statements, all of this is merely reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*), like the sun and the moon.
In the case of reflections in water and so forth; the sense is that the analogy and the subject of the analogy are to be applied in this manner. || 133 ||
Regarding another [state], he said:
"Everything connected with pleasure, pain, and so forth, is mediated by the senses;
thus, having abandoned the senses, one remains established in oneself, abiding in the Self. (134)

By abandoning the conceptualization of distinctions such as "the seer," "the seen," and "the act of seeing," one becomes established in the Self; the meaning is that one becomes one's own true Self. || 134 ||
Regarding another [view], he says: "Everything is the illuminator of knowledge, and the self alone is the illuminator.
Thus, because they possess a single nature, knowledge is manifested within the object of knowledge. (135)
That which is manifest is not separate from manifestation,
and that manifestation is not separate from reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
There is no reflective awareness other than the essential nature of "I."
I am the reflective awareness, whose sole nature is consciousness.
According to this principle, nothing exists or appears apart from Light;
thus, knowledge (*jñāna*), the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and the knower (*jñātṛ*)—this triad has no reality.
Having contemplated everything as consisting solely of Consciousness (*cinmaya*) by means of such characteristics, that very knowledge is itself the object of knowledge and so forth.
The sense is that one becomes established in the knowledge of reality through such means as these. || 135 ||
Regarding another [view], he says:
"The mind, volition, power, and the self—this tetrad, when completely dissolved in the Beloved, then becomes that Bhairava body. (136)

The mind (*mānasa*), the intellect (*manas*), consciousness (*cetanā*), the faculty of cognition (*buddhi*), the power (*śakti*), the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*), and the self (*ātman*)— the individual soul (*jīva*) is said to consist of these as its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). When this quartet consisting of the adjuncts has been dissolved— that is, when it has waned through the removal of the adjuncts of *māyā*— [the soul attains its true state].

When [the impurities] are exhausted, then, by virtue of being reduced to pure consciousness (*ciccheṣatayā*), only light remains, shining like the sun freed from the clouds; through the attainment of this firm experience, the sense is that one becomes Bhairava himself in person. || 136 ||
He spoke another [verse]:
"O Goddess, in brief, one hundred and twelve instructions on the waveless state have been declared; by knowing which, the wise man becomes a knower of knowledge. (137)

Thus, I have stated one hundred and twelve instructions on the *dhāraṇās*; the essential meaning is that by realizing this very [truth], one attains direct conformity (*sārūpya*) with Bhairava. || 137 ||
And here, one who is devoted to any single [practice] becomes Bhairava himself;
by means of speech, he performs actions, bestowing both curses and favors. (138)

One who has attained mastery in any one of these concentrations (dhāraṇās), even though their group of senses remains fallen within the mass of objects of knowledge enveloped by the limiting adjunct of Māyā, performs actions such as cursing or bestowing grace merely by means of speech; and even in that regard, having abandoned those very [actions] through the same unification in meditative absorption (samādhi).
The certainty is that Bhairava, possessing waveless luminosity, becomes directly manifest. || 138 ||

O Goddess, he attains freedom from old age and death, endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others; he becomes the lord of the Yoginīs and the one who brings about all gatherings. 139.

Having attained freedom from old age and death through the firmness gained by practicing the meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) described in passages such as "We have drunk the Soma, we have become immortal," [one attains] higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).
Through the drinking of the *soma* consisting of consciousness, he is the Lord and Master of the Yoginīs—the powers of knowledge, action, bliss, and so forth;

he is the one who brings about union everywhere; he is the Supreme Self, whose nature has rendered this entire aggregate of the known and the knower and all else obsolete, whose body is the utterly pure consciousness, and who consists of non-dual light.
The intended meaning is that he becomes Bhairava. || 139 ||
Even while living, he is liberated; even while acting, he is not tainted.
He is truly one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), for even while seeing, hearing, smelling, and performing such activities, he remains untainted. And so says the Blessed Lord:

Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, breathing; speaking, releasing, grasping, as well as opening and closing the eyes— he who performs actions while taking them up in Brahman and abandoning attachment— (5–8).
"He is not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water" (5.10);
with these and other such verses, he instructs. And likewise in the *Spanda*:
"The outpourings of the vibrations of the qualities (*guṇas*) and so forth arise from their dependence upon the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*)."
"Having attained their own self-nature, they would constantly be non-obstructive to the knower.
This and more has been determined [in the scriptures]. Therefore, it is established that even while performing actions, one is not tainted.
Suspecting a difference because of that very nature, Śrī Bhairavī asked again:
"O Deva, O Maheśvara, if this is indeed the body of Parā... (140)
When such a state has been established, who is it that recites, and what is the recitation? O Mahādeva, who is meditated upon, who is worshipped, and who is satisfied? (141)
58) To whom does the oblation belong, or to whom does the sacrifice belong? What is it, and how is it performed?
This is clear.
Instructing [the disciple] on the determination of the aforementioned inquiry, the illustrious Bhairava said: "O fawn-eyed one, this external procedure is indeed gross. (142)
That meditation which is cultivated again and again upon the supreme reality is indeed the internal process;
whereas external rituals—such as recitation, study, and pilgrimage—are said to be "external" with respect to the supreme reality.
In this context, that internal sound (nāda) itself is the recitation; such is the mantra-nature of the recitation. || 143 ||

Dhyāna is that steady intellect which is changeless and without support; it is the recitation (*japa*) resulting from hearing the sound called *anāhata* with the realization "I am That Brahman. Furthermore, by virtue of having such a mantra as its essence, the mantra itself becomes an auxiliary to the recitation. Although it falls within the sphere of both the knowable and the unknowable, through the power of concentration, it remains like a lamp in a windless place.
That meditation is said to be unwavering intellect; for this very reason, it is changeless and without support.
But meditation is not the imagining of a body with a face, hands, and so forth.
What is called "worship" is not the firm mental resolve directed toward flowers and such ritual offerings;
rather, worship is the dissolution [of the mind] with reverence into the supreme, non-conceptual void. 145.
In the highest ether, in the space of supreme consciousness, dissolution is in truth nothing other than rest; this is the meaning of "worship. || 145 ||
In this context, that state which arises day by day while established in any one of these methods—
the nature of being full— is here called "satisfaction" (tṛpti), which is absolute plenitude.

In this context, when the yogi is established in one of the aforementioned methods of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and has attained firmness in perfected meditative absorption (*samādhi*), that state of fullness— which consists of the experience of the flavor of progressively higher non-conceptual absorption and culminates in the realization of the nature of one's own complete self—
is what is meant by "satisfaction" (*tṛpti*). || 146 ||

In the fire that is the abode of the great void, the elements, sense objects, and so forth, are offered together with the mind; that is the oblation, performed with consciousness as the sacrificial ladle.

In the abode of the Great Void, which is the form of the Void beyond the void, the very nature of Supreme Bhairava— the Fire— in which the entire universe, consisting of the elements, the senses, and the principles (*tattvas*), and composed of conceptualization and mental construction,

is offered as an oblation by that consciousness itself acting as the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) together with the mind that is the cause of the fabrication of distinctions; that [is the true sacrifice].
"Homa is, in reality," [so it is said]. || 147 ||
O Supreme Goddess, sacrifice here is satisfaction characterized by bliss;
it is so called, O Pārvatī, because of the destruction of all fetters and the protection of all. (148)

The immersion into the power of Rudra (*rudraśaktisamāveśa*) is that supreme field (*kṣetra*), which is contemplation (*bhāvanā*). Satisfaction arising from the bliss born of the aforementioned meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is itself the sacrifice (*yāga*), the worship of the deity;
for, because its nature consists in the severing of bonds and protection from worldly existence, it is indeed the immersion into the power of Anāśrita [Śiva], and not merely the physical field.

Furthermore, there is the journey to Kurukṣetra, Dharmakṣetra, and other such places; and the immersion into the power of Rudra (rudraśaktisamāveśa), which is the manifestation of the six powers beginning with omniscience. || 148 ||
Otherwise, what worship could there be for that reality, and who would be satisfied? (149)
The sense is that, in another way, there can be no ritual action such as worship or libation apart from the true reality of non-duality. || 149 ||
He also points out that bathing, which is to be primarily practiced among the rules of right conduct, is as follows:
"For one's own Self, whose essence is independent bliss and pure consciousness, is indeed everywhere;
immersion into that very nature of one's own Self is declared to be 'bathing'. (150)

The meaning is that the primary bath consists of the contemplation of dissolution into that true nature, arising from the experience of the non-dual nature of one's own self as having the essence of independent bliss and pure consciousness, through the practice of the previously described dhāraṇās. || 150 ||
By whatever substances one worships or gratifies the Supreme and the Non-Supreme, and whoever is the worshipper—all that is indeed one; where, then, is the act of worship? (151)

By whatever substances— such as flowers or by milk, sugar-candy, and so forth— the Supreme-Below (parāpara) is worshipped and satisfied; and since the Supreme Bhairava is accompanied by the Supreme Goddess (parādevī), and the one who is the worshipper is indeed the one who is worshipped, where is there any need for worship through this knowledge of reality, given that [worship] on the gross path belongs to everyone?
The sense is that because the object of worship, the act of worship, and so forth, possess that same single nature, there is no difference anywhere. || 51 ||
By her will, the vital breath departs and the individual soul enters; she is of crooked form, long-souled, that Great Goddess, the supreme field, higher than the highest. (152)

At the time of the entry of the *prāṇa*, due to the impact of the *apāna* in the heart and other locations; the detailed esoteric meaning of this verse has been explained in the *Tantrāloka* and other works, and should therefore be understood from those very sources (p.
Since this must be resolved solely from the mouth of the Guru, we have not elaborated upon it here; therefore, it should be forgiven. || 152 ||
Standing as an attendant at this sacrifice consisting of great bliss, one who is possessed by that Goddess shall attain supreme Bhairava. || 153 ||
Twenty-one thousand six hundred times, day and night, the individual soul constantly mutters the mantra "Haṃsa, Haṃsa. (54)
The recitation of the Goddess is prescribed as being extremely difficult to attain at the end of the vital breath;
"at the end of the vital breath" means in the state of final dissolution.
Thus, O Goddess, has this supreme and most excellent nectar been described. || 155 ||
And this must never be disclosed to anyone at all—not to the disciple of another, nor to the wicked, nor to the cruel, nor to one who lacks devotion at the feet of the Guru. (156)
But for those heroes of exalted soul who possess non-conceptualizing minds—
those heroes with non-conceptualizing minds whose doubts are severed and who have transcended Māyā, in whom Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) predominates.
It should be given to the devotees and the group of teachers without any hesitation. || 157 ||

This secret knowledge is to be imparted to those who are devoted to the lineages of gurus, beginning with the Divine Current (divyaugha), the Siddha Current (siddhaugha), and the Human Current (mānavaugha). || 157 ||
O fawn-eyed one, having completely renounced the village, the kingdom, the city, the country, as well as children, wife, and family—all this must be grasped [as unreal]. (158)
(62) O Goddess, what is the use of these unstable things? This supreme wealth is stable;
even one's life-breaths may be given away, but the supreme nectar must not be given. 159.

By renouncing unstable wealth such as kingdoms and the like— which does not follow one beyond death— one should acquire this stable wealth that follows one, which has unsurpassed happiness as its fruit, and which must be given in every way to the designated worthy recipients.
O Lord of gods, O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, I am fully satisfied;
today I have grasped the essence of the Rudrayāmala Tantra.
"Today the heart of all the various powers has been known," having said this, the Goddess, filled with joy, embraced Śiva around his neck.
These verses have clear explanations; therefore, enough with further elaboration. || 160-161 ||
Thus ends the Yoga Treatise named the Śrī Vijñānabhairava. (p.
63) Having obtained a mere fraction of insight through the grace of the Śrīvidyā, [I have extracted] from the Trika scriptures...
Having thoroughly churned and reflected upon it for the purpose of compiling that very essence, [I have composed] this most extensive work. || 1 ||

In the *Vijñānabhairava*, [this work] which awakens one to the meaning of the words on the hidden path, is proclaimed for the sake of protection from falling into the terrible abyss of worldly existence, which is like a dense darkness. (2)
In the month of Madhu, on the day of the new moon, in the year [measured] by the Vedas, the seven sages, the Vedas, and the end of the Yuga,
Bhaṭṭānanda caused this Vijñānakaumudī to bloom.
This commentary on the Vijñānabhairava, titled *Vijñānakaumudī*, is completed.
It is the work of the venerable Kashmiri Bhaṭṭāraka Ānanda.

By one endowed with the vigor of right discernment, for the sake of the performance of action. || 1 ||
Having deliberated with his principal ministers who were devoted to righteousness, the illustrious sovereign of Kaśmīra established [this work],
which is filled with spiritual knowledge and realized wisdom.

There, by the virtuous who enter upon a life of spiritual sustenance (ājīva), having taken refuge under the supervision of Mukunda and Rāma, this [place] is [attained].
